questions.q: What speedup does Grover's algorithm provide over classical unstructured search?
options: No speedup; it is purely illustrative
A quadratic speedup: roughly O(root N) quantum steps vs. O(N) classical steps
An exponential speedup for every search space size
It only works faster for already-sorted lists
questions.explain: Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among N unsorted items in roughly O(root(N/M)) iterations, a quadratic speedup over the O(N/M) checks classical search needs on average.

questions.q: In the 2-qubit example circuit, what does `qc.cz(0, 1)` (the oracle) do?
options: It measures qubit 0 and collapses the state
It phase-flips only the marked state `|11>`, leaving all probabilities at 0.25 and revealing nothing via measurement
It swaps the values of qubit 0 and qubit 1
It immediately sets the amplitude of `|11>` to 1
questions.explain: A controlled-Z flips the sign of the |11> amplitude only. Right after the oracle, every outcome is still equally likely (probability 0.25 each) — only the hidden phase has changed, which the diffuser later converts into a measurable probability boost.

questions.q: For N=4 items with exactly 1 marked item, what is the verified result of running exactly one Grover iteration (oracle + diffuser) starting from uniform superposition?
options: The marked state has probability 0.5, same as one unmarked state
The marked state `|11>` has probability exactly 1.0, with every other state at probability 0
All 4 states remain equally likely at 0.25
The circuit requires 4 iterations to reach any improvement
questions.explain: This is the special, exact case: for N=4 and M=1, the optimal iteration count given by (pi/4)*root(N/M) works out to exactly 1, producing a perfect, deterministic amplification to the marked state with probability 1.0.

questions.q: What happens if you run more Grover iterations than the optimal count?
options: The success probability keeps increasing indefinitely
Nothing changes; extra iterations are harmless no-ops
The success probability can decrease again, since the oracle-diffuser step is a periodic rotation that can overshoot the marked state
The circuit becomes invalid and Qiskit raises an error
questions.explain: Grover's operator is a geometric rotation in state space. Rotations are periodic, so iterating past the optimal count rotates the state past the marked outcome and back toward unmarked ones, decreasing success probability.

questions.q: What is the practical advantage of using `qiskit_algorithms.Grover` with `AmplificationProblem` instead of hand-building the oracle and diffuser every time?
options: It avoids needing a quantum computer at all
It automatically builds the matching diffuser and determines the iteration count from your oracle, instead of you deriving these by hand for every problem
It eliminates the need for any oracle whatsoever
It guarantees a classical, not quantum, speedup
questions.explain: AmplificationProblem packages your oracle so Grover can automatically construct the corresponding diffuser and compute a good iteration count, which is exactly what you did by hand in the lesson's minimal example, generalized to arbitrary oracles.
